context.candidate: Please enter your passcode to confirm this payment.

task: Footer line telling the person how to spot a real email.

context.candidate: We will never ask you for your passcode or card details by email.

expected: A statement about what we never do, not a request; required in every transactional email.

task: Subject of the new-device security email.

context.candidate: A new phone logged in to your account

expected: States the event without alarm and without accusing.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a push showing the balance on a lock screen.
expected: The deterministic layer passes it; the judge must reject it. A push is read by whoever is looking at the phone, and the balance is not theirs to see.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: three facts stacked into one block.

context.candidate: Your money is safe. This card will stop working for good, and we will send you a new one. The replacement is free and usually arrives in 3 to 5 working days.

expected: Must FAIL: the same words in one block force the person to read all of it to find the fact that matters to them.

task: Two short, tightly linked sentences in one paragraph.

context.candidate: It takes 3 steps and about 2 minutes. You will need your card.

expected: Allowed: two sentences are fine when they are linked and both short.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: two sentences that run long in one paragraph.

context.candidate: Your payment of 150 € to Luis García is on its way and should arrive today. We will send you another message as soon as it lands in their account.

expected: Must FAIL: two sentences are allowed only when both are short; this pair is a wall in two lines.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: US payment vocabulary.

context.candidate: Use ACH to send money to your account.

expected: Must FAIL: wrong market. Word-boundary matching, so ‘reach’ and ‘each’ are untouched.

task: A word that contains the banned acronym.

context.candidate: We could not reach our systems just now.

expected: Passes: the old substring matching would have flagged ‘reach’ as ACH.

task: A word that contains a banned term.
expected: Passes: ‘provisional’ is not ‘provision’.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: login used as a verb.
expected: Must FAIL: ‘log in’ is the verb; ‘login’ is only a noun.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: an ampersand in body copy.

context.candidate: Your cards & accounts are up to date.

expected: Must FAIL: the ampersand belongs to tight labels only.

task: An ampersand in a tight label.
expected: Passes: the check is surface-aware.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: British spelling.
expected: Must FAIL: the baseline is American English.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: hype as a claim.
expected: Must FAIL: show it is simple, do not assert it.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: Title Case on a button.
expected: Must FAIL: Vanker writes in sentence case.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a range written with a hyphen.

context.candidate: It usually arrives in 3-5 working days.

expected: Must FAIL: in a bank a hyphen between figures reads as a minus sign.

task: A range written correctly.

context.candidate: It usually arrives in 3 to 5 working days.

expected: Ranges take to.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: an exclamation mark.

context.candidate: Your money is on its way!

expected: Must FAIL: Vanker never shouts, not even in success.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a Latin abbreviation.

context.candidate: Some payments, e.g. direct debits, take longer.

expected: Must FAIL: write for example.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: an em dash in product copy.

context.candidate: Your money is safe — nothing has left your account.

expected: Must FAIL: use a comma, a full stop, or parentheses.

task: A format placeholder is uppercase by definition.
expected: Passes: the ALL CAPS rule does not apply to a format example.

task: A sentence that repeats a proper noun.

context.candidate: The account belongs to “Luis M. García”, not “Luis García”.

expected: Passes: a repeated name is not Title Case. This case exists because the sweep flagged it.

task: Link to the privacy policy from a consent checkbox.
expected: Names the destination and works read out of context.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: the emptiest link there is.
expected: Must FAIL: a list of links reading ‘here’ is a list of identical, meaningless entries.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: the most common empty link.
expected: Must FAIL: it names the act, not the destination.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a raw URL as link text in an email.
expected: Must FAIL: a bare URL is what a fake looks like; name the destination.

task: Link that opens a document.
expected: Says it leaves and what it opens.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: the sentence period inside the link.
expected: Must FAIL: the trailing punctuation stays outside the link.

task: Link to a statement from an email.
expected: Short, names the destination, same wording everywhere it appears.

task: Line telling the person when a payment arrives.
expected: Day month year, written out, absolute because it has a consequence.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a numeric date.
expected: Must FAIL: 03/04 is 3 April to a European reader and 4 March to an American one.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: month-first order.
expected: Must FAIL: the format is day month year.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a relative day other than today.
expected: Must FAIL: only Today is relative; every other day shows its date.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: money in shorthand.
expected: Must FAIL: a person’s money is never shorthand.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: the lazy plural.
expected: Must FAIL: write the sentence so it works for one and for several.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: vague timing.
expected: Must FAIL: a measured range, or nothing.

task: The phrase that must not be caught by the vague-timing rule.

context.candidate: We will be back as soon as we can.

expected: Passes: ‘as soon as we can’ is an honest statement of not knowing, not vague timing.

task: A payment timing that depends on a bank being open.

context.candidate: It usually arrives in 3 to 5 working days.

expected: Says working days: the difference between calendar and working days is a weekend.

task: A payment cutoff.

context.candidate: Payments sent after 4:00 pm arrive the next working day.

expected: 12-hour with am/pm; a cutoff that is ambiguous by an hour is a payment that misses it.

task: Message when a direct debit is returned for lack of funds.
expected: Describes the event. The person is not named by their money situation.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a label for a person in difficulty.
expected: Must FAIL: it turns a circumstance into an identity, in a message the person did not ask for.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: moralizing about money.
expected: Must FAIL: a bank does not know why, and guessing is wrong in the cases that matter most.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: assumed gender.
expected: Must FAIL: singular they.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: the longer form of the same assumption.

context.candidate: Ask him or her to confirm the transfer.

expected: Must FAIL: singular they. Found while testing the check.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a term with a history.

context.candidate: This card is on our blacklist.

expected: Must FAIL: blocked list.

task: Label of an accessibility setting.
expected: Names the feature, not the person who might need it.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: naming the person instead of the feature.
expected: Must FAIL: name the feature. This case exists because the check first missed this surface.

task: A legitimate use of a word the list touches.

context.candidate: The connection was poor, so we could not reach our systems.

expected: Passes: the list names ‘the poor’ as a label for people, not the adjective.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: comparing one customer with others.

context.candidate: You saved more than 60% of customers this month.

expected: Code passes it; the judge must reject it. A compliment at the top of the ranking is a judgement at the bottom, on something nobody chose to enter.

task: Illustration above the empty transactions state.
expected: Decorative: the heading already says it, so the alt is empty and the attribute is present.

task: Icon-only button that freezes a card.
expected: Names the function, not the snowflake.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: the redundant prefix.

context.candidate: Image of a graph showing spending

expected: Must FAIL: the screen reader already says it is an image.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a file name left as alt.
expected: Must FAIL: this is what a person hears when the attribute is missing or lazy.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a one-word alt that says nothing.
expected: Must FAIL: name what the person would miss.

task: Alt for the monthly spending chart.

context.candidate: Spending by category this month, with groceries the largest.

expected: What it shows and the takeaway; the figures themselves are text elsewhere on the screen.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: an amount that exists only in the image.
expected: Must FAIL: money is real text on the screen, never only in a picture or its description.

task: Alt for a help screenshot.

context.candidate: The Cards screen, with the Frozen switch turned on.

expected: Describes the step, not the pixels.

task: Badge on the messages tab.
expected: A count, and nothing else.

task: Badge when the count is large.
expected: Capped rather than squeezed into a circle.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a badge showing zero.
expected: Must FAIL: nothing to clear means no badge.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a marketing badge.
expected: Must FAIL: a badge counts things. Marketing borrows the language of ‘something of yours is waiting’ for something nobody asked for.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: money in a badge.
expected: Must FAIL: a badge counts things; an amount is text on the screen.

task: Filter chip on the transactions screen.
expected: Names the value; parallel with the other chips in the row.

task: Filter chip carrying an amount range.
expected: The one control where a figure belongs, because the figure is the value being chosen.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a chip that names the act.
expected: Must FAIL: a verb makes it look like a button. The label is ‘Date’.

task: Placeholder of the global search field.
expected: Names the scope: the most useful thing the only naming a search field gets can do.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a placeholder that names nothing.
expected: Must FAIL: it wastes the one chance to say what can be found here.

task: Nothing found for a query.
expected: Echoes the query in the person’s own words and names the scope; the way out is a button.

task: Nothing found because a filter is still on.

context.candidate: No transactions match “ana” in the last 30 days

expected: Names the filter responsible: the most common dead end in a banking app.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: the empty answer.
expected: Must FAIL: it answers nothing and offers nothing.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: blaming the spelling.

context.candidate: Nothing here. Check your spelling and try again.

expected: Must FAIL: the query is echoed so the person can see it for themselves.

task: Line stating how many results and in what.
expected: Count and scope, with the query echoed.

task: Button that clears the filter blocking the results.
expected: The way out is a button, not an instruction in the sentence.

task: The chosen payment date falls on a Saturday.

context.candidate: 4 September is a Saturday, so your payment will arrive on 6 September.

expected: States the reason and the resulting date. Nothing moves silently.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a date changed without saying what happens.
expected: Must FAIL: no reason and no consequence, so the payment arrives on a day nobody expects.

task: Cutoff stated before the person picks a date.

context.candidate: Payments sent after 4:00 pm arrive the next working day.

expected: The cutoff is part of the date, and it is said before choosing, not after.

task: The written echo under a completed date group.
expected: Written out, so someone who typed 03 and 04 sees which reading we took.

task: Error when one part of the date group is empty.
expected: Names the part, not the whole group.

task: Error for a date that does not exist.
expected: States what is expected, without blaming.

task: Error when an age rule is not met.

context.candidate: You must be 18 or older to open a Vanker account.

expected: A rule, not a judgement: never ‘you are too young’.

task: Error for a date of birth in the future.

context.candidate: A date of birth cannot be in the future.

expected: States what is expected; the negative is spelled out.

task: Confirmation carrying an amount and a recipient.

context.candidate: Your payment of {amount} € to {recipient} is on its way.

expected: One complete sentence with named variables inside it.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a positional placeholder.

context.candidate: Your payment of %s to %s is on its way.

expected: Must FAIL: a translator has to be able to move a variable, and a positional token in a different word order is a guess.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: indexed placeholders.
expected: Must FAIL: name the variables.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a variable glued into a word.
expected: Must FAIL: plural rules differ by language; use a plural-aware string.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: pointing at a position on the screen.

context.candidate: Tap the button on the right to continue.

expected: Must FAIL: layouts mirror in right-to-left languages and a screen reader user has no left. Name the control.

task: The same instruction, naming the control.
expected: Names the control, so it survives mirroring, reflow, and a screen reader.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a sentence assembled from fragments.
expected: Code cannot see this: the fragment is well formed on its own. The judge must reject it, because a sentence assembled at runtime is invisible to every other check in the system.

task: Line stating the category we assigned to a payment.

context.candidate: We sorted this as Groceries. Change category.

expected: Presented as our reading, with the correction in the same copy.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a guessed category presented as a fact.
expected: Must FAIL: categorization is inference, and someone will act on it as though we had checked it.

task: Comparison with the previous month.

context.candidate: You spent 32% more than in August.

expected: Reports rather than grades, and names the baseline.

task: Total for a month that has not finished.

context.candidate: You have spent 420 € so far this month.

expected: Labels the incomplete period; a running month is not comparable with a finished one.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a verdict instead of a report.
expected: Must FAIL: a chart reports; it does not grade.

task: Label of the grouped tail of a breakdown.
expected: Grouping is allowed only because it opens and lists what is inside.

task: A payment we could not categorize.

context.candidate: We could not sort 2 payments into a category. Change category.

expected: Says so rather than sweeping them into Other.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: copy describing a chart with a truncated axis.
expected: Code passes it: the format is right and no term is banned. The judge must reject it, because the claim contradicts the figures it carries, which is what a truncated axis does visually.

task: Rate line before confirming a conversion.

context.candidate: 1 € = 1,0745 USD. Our markup: 0,5% over the ECB rate.

expected: The rate with its markup: a rate alone tells the person nothing they can act on.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: the rate with no markup.
expected: Must FAIL: a rate reads as a fact about the world, not as our margin.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: advertising no commission while charging a spread.
expected: Must FAIL: the cost is in the rate, so the absence of a fee is not the absence of a cost.

task: The cost of the conversion, in euros.
expected: The markup expressed as money, because nobody converts a spread in their head.

task: The received amount when an intermediary can deduct.

context.candidate: Ana receives about 107,45 USD. Their bank may deduct a fee we cannot see.

expected: An estimate stated as an estimate, with the reason. We never promise an amount we do not control.

task: How long the quoted rate holds.
expected: A fact about the quote, never a countdown that pressures.

task: Conversion that cannot happen until the market opens.

context.candidate: Currency markets are closed until Monday, so this will convert on 6 September.

expected: Says when, with a concrete date, before the person commits.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a rate that changed without saying so.

context.candidate: Your transfer was sent at the current rate.

expected: Code passes it: no rate, no banned term. The judge must reject it, because a payment that went out at a rate the person never saw is the worst outcome of this flow.

task: Acknowledgement shown as soon as a complaint is sent.

context.candidate:
We have your complaint. Your reference is VNK-4821.

We will answer within 15 working days. If we need longer, we will tell you before then and explain why.

expected: Reference on screen, timeframe up front, and what happens if it slips.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: an acknowledgement that says nothing.

context.candidate: We have your complaint. We will be in touch.

expected: Must FAIL: no reference and no timeframe, so the person has nothing to hold us to.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a defensive refusal.

context.candidate: Unfortunately, as per our terms and conditions, this fee is non-refundable.

expected: Must FAIL: a complaint answered defensively is a complaint that escalates.

task: An answer that declines the claim.

context.candidate:
We are not refunding the 40 € fee, because it was charged for a same-day transfer you confirmed on 2 September.

If you are not happy with this, you can take it to the Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) body for free, and we will help you do it.

expected: States the outcome plainly with its reason, and names the free escalation route in the same message.

task: Telling the person we need longer, before the limit.

context.candidate: We need longer to answer, so we will come back to you by 20 October.

expected: Announced before the limit, with the new date and the reason.

task: The route for someone locked out of the app.

context.candidate: You can also complain by phone or email, without signing in.

expected: Someone locked out cannot complain in the app, and the lockout may be the complaint.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a survey after a complaint.

context.candidate: Your complaint is closed. How would you rate your experience with us?

expected: Code passes it: no defensive term, no missing reference on this surface. The judge must reject it, because asking someone to rate us at the end of a complaint is the flow serving itself.

task: An acronym expanded on first use, as the glossary requires.

context.candidate: You can take it to the Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) body for free.

expected: Passes: an acronym expansion is Title Case by definition and the system requires it. The strict audit flagged this as Title Case, which was a fault in the check.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: an error title with a written-out noise.

context.candidate: Your transfer did not go through. Oooh.

expected: Must FAIL: 'Oooh' is a noise, not information. Found by breaking the checker on purpose.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: an error body ending in an interjection.

context.candidate: A technical problem stopped it, and no money has left your account. Yeah.

expected: Must FAIL: 'Yeah' is enthusiasm the person does not share, on a screen about their money.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: a button label with a repeated letter.
expected: Must FAIL: a typo is a shape, and a shape is what deterministic code is for.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: two actions in one button label.
expected: Must FAIL: one button does one thing. 'or', 'and' and 'then' in a label mean two buttons were merged.

task: A date format placeholder, which legitimately repeats letters.
expected: Must PASS: the repeated-letter check is exempt by shape (all caps, slashes), not by a list of exceptions.

task: The correct button label for the same error screen.
expected: Must PASS: one verb, one action, no noise. Pins the fix so a later rule cannot break it.

task: A disclosure that names the scheme the law obliges us to name.

context.candidate: Your eligible deposits are protected up to 100.000 € per depositor by the Deposit Guarantee Scheme.

expected: Must PASS: a named entity is Title Case because that is its name. compliance/disclosures.md requires it verbatim, so the case check cannot punish it.

task: A title and a body arriving in one string, separated by a line break.

context.candidate:
Your card is on its way
It usually arrives in 3 to 5 working days.

expected: Must PASS: a slot break is a sentence break. The body's first word is not Title Case.

task: In-app notification: a subscription the person pays monthly is going up in price. Say what changes, by how much, from when, and where to act.

context.candidate:
Your Netflix subscription is going up
From 14 September you will pay 15,99 € a month instead of 12,99 €. You can review or cancel it in Subscriptions.

expected: Validated 01/09. Names the merchant, both amounts, the date and the route to act. No alarm, no blame, no advice on whether to keep it.

task: Empty state for the Statements screen in the first month, when no statement exists yet. Say what will appear and when, without making the person feel they are missing something.
expected: An all-caught-up state, not a first-use one: no CTA, neutral tone, says when the first statement arrives. THE PERMANENT GENERATION SLOT: it never receives a context.candidate. If every case carries one, judge.py generate has nothing to do and the generation path rots unnoticed. Approved copy for this screen, if it is ever needed, goes in its own case with its own id.

task: NEGATIVE CASE: an error screen that never says whose side the problem is on.

context.candidate:
Your transfer did not go through.

A technical problem stopped it, and no money has left your account.

expected: Must FAIL: rule 2 of system-errors.md. The money is accounted for and the sentence is well formed, which is why every other check passed it. Found by the judge on the app's own worked example.

task: An error screen that owns the failure.

context.candidate:
We could not complete your payment.

Something did not work on our side.

We do not know yet whether the payment went through, and we will tell you as soon as we do.

expected: Must PASS: names our side and accounts for the money without promising an outcome we do not know.

task: A session expiry, which is not a failure and has no side to name.

context.candidate:
We logged you out.

We do this after a while without activity, to keep your account safe.

Your money is safe, and nothing you were doing has been lost.

expected: Must PASS: the attribution check asks only of screens that report a failure. An expired session is not one, which the strict audit caught the day the check was written too broadly.
